How Utah assesses residential property

Market value on January 1 drives the Utah tax bill, and a primary residence is taxed on only 55% of it after a 45% reduction. The rule sits in Utah Code 59-2-103, which sets one uniform rate of valuation for taxable property unless a specific law changes it.

Most Utah homes get the reduction, subject to a few limits.

  • Land counts only up to one acre for each residential unit.
  • A household gets it on a single primary residence. Homes lived in by a tenant as a primary residence are an exception.
  • A property that turns residential after January 1 can still qualify once it is lived in for 183 or more consecutive days that year.
  • Transient use and condominiums in rental pools do not qualify.

Which office does what

Three county offices handle your bill. The assessor sets value, the auditor mails the valuation notice, and the treasurer takes payment. Call whichever one matches your question.

All counties follow the same statewide calendar, but forms, payment portals and office hours differ. Notice rules for tax sales vary by county class: first class counties post on a website and smaller ones use newspapers. Owners of a rural house should look at the county treasurer's page for payment methods and any local deferral process.

The valuation notice

Every owner on the assessment roll gets a valuation and tax change notice from the county auditor, mailed by July 22. Utah Code 59-2-919.1 sets the timing: at least 10 days ahead of the county board of equalization meeting and ahead of any taxing entity hearing on a proposed rate increase.

Look on it for the assessor's value, the taxable value, last year's tax, the tax at the current rate and appeal instructions with the deadline. Residential notices add a line about deferral for owners who are 65 or older, disabled, or in extreme hardship. Owners can elect electronic notice, and the county falls back to mail if it can't confirm receipt.

If you're selling, read this notice before listing or signing a contract. The value on it feeds next year's tax bill, and the appeal clock starts when it is mailed.

How to appeal your valuation

File your application with the county board of equalization by the later of September 15 or 45 days after the auditor mails the valuation notice, as set out in Utah Code 59-2-1004. Expect a decision from the board within 60 days of the application, though the Tax Commission can extend that.

If the county board's answer isn't acceptable, the next level is the State Tax Commission. Under 59-2-1006, the notice of appeal goes to the county auditor within 30 days after the board's final action. The commission may admit more evidence and adjust the value. It weighs the accuracy and comparability of evidence, including sale prices of comparable property under contract as of the lien date, and offering prices of property that was listed but did not sell.

The commission must decide real property appeals by March 1 of the following year. It also adjusts values when the property deviates by 5% or more, up or down, from comparable properties after an equalization issue is raised.

Utah property tax dates

Tax notices go out by November 1, taxes are due November 30, and a payment that arrives or is postmarked later is delinquent. Here is the calendar a prospective seller needs.

DateWhat happens
January 1Valuation date for market value, and the date the annual tax lien attaches
By July 22Valuation notice mailed by the county auditor
September 15 or 45 days after noticeAppeal deadline to the county board, whichever is later
September 1Common deadline for abatement, senior deferral and exemption claims
By November 1County treasurer mails the tax notice
November 30Taxes due, moved to the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday
By December 31Notice of delinquency to unpaid owners
January 31Last day to pay delinquent tax and penalty before interest runs from January 1

Late payment penalties and interest

Miss the due date and the bill picks up a penalty of 2.5% of the delinquent amount or $10, whichever is greater. Clear the taxes, notice charges and penalty by the following January 31 and the penalty falls to 1% or $10.

After January 31, interest runs on an annual basis from the January 1 following delinquency. The rate is 6% plus the federal funds target rate on that January 1, but never less than 7% or more than 10%, as written in 59-2-1331. Each further year of delinquency adds its own interest until the taxes are paid or the property goes to a tax sale.

Before the delinquency date the treasurer will take partial payments of $10 or more on the current year. Someone paying only part of a bill can say how to divide it among tax, assessments, past-due district fees and other notice charges.

Tax notice charges

Counties add extra items to the property tax bill called tax notice charges, and these rank equal to the tax. Utah Code 59-2-1317 lists examples such as liens for unpaid municipal water, unpaid abatement fees, special district fees, irrigation district charges and assessment area payments.

Unpaid charges can set a tax sale in motion just as unpaid tax does. The bill has to carry a warning when prior taxes or charges are delinquent on the parcel, plus a notice about assessment area charges that paying one bill may not pay off the full amount owed or release the lien.

The total on the bill may hide some of this. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure that includes charges, interest and penalties before closing.

Relief programs for Utah homeowners

Counties administer abatements, deferrals and exemptions, and State Tax Commission Publication 36 sets the income and age tests. Current amounts follow.

  • Homeowner low-income abatement: up to $1,412 for owner-occupants with 2025 income under $44,221 who meet an age, disability or prior-credit test.
  • Mandatory senior deferral: for owners age 75 or older with income not over $88,442. It carries interest at half the normal rate and must be renewed yearly.
  • Service-connected disability exemption: up to $535,459 of taxable value on a residence for anyone with at least a 10% service-connected disability.
  • Blind exemption: up to $11,500 of taxable value, with no age or income test.
  • Deadline for most claims: September 1.

A county legislative body can also accept less than the full tax due or defer it when it finds that serves the best interests of the owner, the county and the state, under 59-2-1347. Any deferred amount becomes a recorded lien, bears interest, and is due when the property is sold or otherwise conveyed.

Selling with property taxes owed

A lien for each year's tax attaches on January 1, which means the closing agent normally pays off any balance from your proceeds after checking the figure with the treasurer.

A change in ownership also triggers a residential exemption check. Under 59-2-103.5, after an ownership interest changes the county assessor sends the owner a notice, and the new owner must return a signed residential declaration within 90 days. A second notice gives 30 more days before the exemption is lost for that year. A seller who stops living in the home should also notify the county board of equalization that the residence no longer qualifies, unless they moved to another primary residence that qualifies.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Common tax problems for sellers

Three problems come up again and again: a deferral lien, a delinquent bill nobody opened, and an exemption that changed after a transfer. The fix differs for each.

  • Deferral lien: deferred tax plus interest comes due when you sell. Get the balance from the county.
  • Delinquent bill: paying by January 31 holds the penalty at 1%. Otherwise line up a payoff before a tax sale draws near.
  • Lost exemption: file the declaration inside the county's window, or appeal before the September 15 cutoff.
  • Inherited house: bills may keep going to the late owner, so change the mailing address.

When the house also needs work or has turned into a burden, an as-is cash sale can clear these balances at closing without the owner fixing anything first.

Frequently asked questions

When are Utah property taxes due?

Bills are due November 30 (the next business day when that lands on a weekend or holiday). Notices arrive by November 1. Anything paid or postmarked later is delinquent.

What is the Utah residential property tax exemption?

Primary residences are taxed on 55% of market value after a 45% reduction. The break covers up to one acre per unit and one primary home per household.

How long do I have to appeal my Utah property value?

Whichever is later: September 15, or 45 days from the auditor's mailing of your valuation notice. You then have 30 days to take a board decision to the State Tax Commission.

What is the penalty for paying Utah property tax late?

The greater of 2.5% of what's late or $10. Paying everything by January 31 cuts that to 1%, and interest from January 1 starts after that date.

Can I defer my Utah property tax?

Some can. Owners 75 and older who meet income tests qualify for a mandatory senior deferral, and counties may allow others. What you defer is recorded as a lien and paid on sale.

What the Utah homestead exemption means

In Utah the word covers two separate protections: a creditor protection for equity in your home, and a property tax reduction for primary residences. They sit in different parts of the Utah Code and are handled by different offices.

The creditor protection is in the Utah Exemptions Act, Utah Code 78B-5-503 and 78B-5-504, and it is enforced in court. The tax reduction is in Utah Code 59-2-103 and 59-2-103.5, and your county assessor applies it. A homeowner preparing to sell may care about both, and mixing them up leads to wrong assumptions about who to call.

How much of a Utah home is protected from creditors

A primary personal residence is exempt up to $42,000 in value, and other property up to $5,000. Those figures are adjusted for inflation each year, so check the current numbers with the state.

Utah homestead exemption amounts
Protected propertyAmount
Primary personal residence, one owner$42,000
Other property, one owner$5,000
Jointly owned primary residence, household maximum$84,000
Other property, household maximum$10,000
Land counted with the homeUp to one acre reasonably necessary for its use

A primary personal residence is a dwelling or mobile home where you and your household live, plus the surrounding land up to one acre. A household here means people related by blood or marriage who live together as an economic unit.

Debts the homestead does not protect against

The homestead is not a shield against every claim. Section 78B-5-503 lists the exceptions, and a lender or the county can still reach the house in these cases.

  • Statutory liens for property taxes and assessments.
  • Security interests and judicial liens for the purchase price.
  • Judicial liens for unpaid child support or maintenance.
  • Consensual liens created by a contract, such as a mortgage or trust deed.
  • Calls or assessments on water rights used for the homestead.
  • Property acquired through criminal activity.

In practice the exemption matters most to an owner with unsecured debt, such as a judgment or a credit card balance, who wants to know whether the house can be forced to a sale.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Utah house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to claim the homestead

Under Utah Code 78B-5-504 you claim it by filing a signed and acknowledged declaration with the recorder of the county where the property sits. You can also serve it on the sheriff or officer running an execution before the time stated in the notice of execution.

The declaration must include the following items:

  • A claim of exemption and, if married, a statement that your spouse has not filed one.
  • A description of the property and an estimated cash value.
  • The amount of homestead you are claiming.
  • The name, age and address of any spouse and dependents.

If you do not file or serve it as required, title passes to the purchaser at the execution sale free of homestead rights. For married owners, a conveyance, security interest or contract to convey homestead property is valid only if both spouses sign, which also matters when you sell.

Can a Utah homestead be sold at an execution sale?

Homestead property cannot be sold at execution unless a bid exceeds the declared exemption amount. A sale is subject to the debtor's right of redemption under Rule 69C of the Utah Rules of Civil Procedure, and if there is a deficiency the property cannot be taken again to cover it.

An owner facing an execution sale should get advice from a Utah attorney about how the proceeds are divided.

Money from selling a Utah homestead

Sale proceeds up to the exemption amount at the time of sale are exempt from levy, execution or other process for one year after you receive them. A sale also does not stop you from claiming or buying another homestead.

That one year window is useful when you sell and plan to buy elsewhere. Keep the closing statement and deposit records together so you can show where the exempt money came from.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Utah houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

The primary residential exemption for property tax

Utah allows a 45% reduction in the fair market value of residential property for a calendar year, so a qualifying home is taxed on 55% of its value. The exemption applies to one primary residence per household and to no more than one acre of land per residential unit.

The home must be a primary domicile occupied for at least 183 consecutive days in a calendar year, by the owner or by a full-time tenant. Vacation and second homes do not qualify. A home that becomes residential after January 1 can qualify as part-year property if it is used as a residence for 183 or more consecutive days that year.

  • 90 days: time to return the primary residence declaration after the county's notice.
  • 30 days: time to file after a second notice, or lose the exemption for that year.
  • September 15: application deadline, and late applications cannot be accepted.
  • 183 days: consecutive days of occupancy needed.
  • November 30: property tax due date.

Missing the deadline can mean being taxed on 100% of market value for that year.

The exemption after a sale

The exemption does not carry over to new owners, who must file their own application. Starting January 1, 2027, an ownership change, including a deed, a trust transfer or a name update, requires a TC-473A filing with the county board of equalization.

Under Utah Code 59-2-103.5, an owner who no longer qualifies must tell the county on a form and declare the change on the Utah income tax return. That notice is not required when the owner moves to a new primary residence and qualifies for it.

  • Check your valuation notice, mailed each year on or before July 22, to see whether the exemption is applied.
  • Tell the county if the home stops being your primary residence.
  • Expect the buyer to file a new application.
  • Pay or prorate the November 30 tax at closing.

If the house is rented out

A rental can still qualify if it is a tenant's primary residence. Utah Code 59-2-103 allows the exemption for each residential property that is a tenant's primary residence, and the owner files a declaration under penalty of perjury.

The assessor may ask for a signed lease. If that falls short, the assessor may ask for an insurance policy and then a federal tax return showing rental profit or loss. The county may not contact the tenant directly. The owner's own home has to be a separate primary residence for the one per household rule.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Other Utah property tax relief

Utah has several relief programs beyond the 45% exemption, and counties make the first call on eligibility. Each has its own form number.

  • Homeowner's tax credit: form TC-90H.
  • Renter refund: form TC-90CB.
  • Low-income abatement: form TC-90L.
  • Delinquent tax deferral or settlement: form PT-33, with PT-33A for a lienholder agreement.
  • Active-duty armed forces exemption (PT-22), veteran with a disability exemption (PT-25) and blind persons exemption (PT-31).

The valuation notice must also tell owners who are 65 or older, disabled or facing extreme hardship that they may be able to defer tax on a primary residence. Deferred amounts are a lien, which matters at closing.

Selling a Utah house for cash

If the house has tax due, judgment liens or a mortgage behind, the homestead does not stop a sale and does not erase those claims. It protects equity from certain creditors, and the proceeds stay protected for a year.

Cash Home Buyers buys Utah houses as-is, including houses with inherited title, tenants or delinquent tax. If you are weighing a sale, tell us what liens or notices are recorded and we can look at the numbers with your title company.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Utah homestead exemption?

$42,000 for a primary personal residence and $5,000 for other property, with a household maximum of $84,000 for a jointly owned primary residence. The figures are adjusted for inflation each year, so confirm the current amounts.

Do I have to file a homestead declaration in Utah?

Yes, to claim it. Utah Code 78B-5-504 calls for a signed, acknowledged declaration with the county recorder, or service on the officer running an execution before the time in the notice of execution. Without it, title can pass to the buyer at an execution sale free of homestead rights.

What is the Utah primary residential exemption deadline?

September 15 for applications. Late applications cannot be accepted, and missing the date can mean being taxed on 100% of market value for that year.

Is the Utah homestead exemption transferable to a buyer?

No. The property tax exemption does not carry over to new owners. A buyer files a new application, and from January 1, 2027, an ownership change requires form TC-473A with the county board of equalization.

Are my sale proceeds protected after I sell my Utah home?

Partly. Proceeds up to the exemption amount at the time of sale are exempt from levy or execution for one year after you receive them, and you may claim or buy another homestead.

title: Utah Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Utah Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Utah Estate and Inheritance Tax sale

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Utah?

Does Utah charge an estate or inheritance tax?

No. Utah's inheritance tax was repealed and ended after December 31, 2004, and no Utah inheritance tax return needs to be filed.

Utah also does not require an Inheritance Tax Waiver, a document some states ask for before a title can move. For an heir who plans to sell a parent's house, that removes one step. The old tax sat in Utah Code Title 59, Chapter 11.

Utah never layered a separate estate tax on top. You will not find a Utah death tax line on the closing statement for an inherited house.

Why Utah's tax disappeared

The old Utah levy was a pick-up tax. It collected only the slice of federal estate tax that Washington allowed as a credit for state death taxes, so once that federal credit ended, the state had nothing left to hang the tax on.

A short list of states still levy an inheritance tax on the person who receives property: Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Other states have their own estate tax. Utah is on neither list. If the person who died, or the heir, has ties to one of those states, an estate attorney should check whether another state's tax applies.

When the federal estate tax matters

Federal estate tax only reaches estates above a high threshold, set at $13,990,000 for deaths in 2025 and $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026.

Add the gross estate, adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption. If that total passes the threshold for the year of death, a return is due. Most simple estates, such as those holding mainly cash or publicly traded securities, do not need to file. A surviving spouse can receive the unused exemption through a portability election, but only on a timely filed estate tax return.

The IRS estate tax page has the current thresholds.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Utah house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Tax when heirs sell an inherited Utah house

What most heirs actually run into is income tax on gain above the stepped-up basis, not an estate tax.

Your basis in an inherited home is usually its market value on the day the owner died, or the alternate valuation date if the estate elected it. If a Form 706 was filed, the value on that return controls. Selling soon after the death at about that value leaves little gain. Holding the house for years, or renting it out, can create more.

  • Get a date-of-death appraisal early, since it fixes your basis.
  • Keep records of repairs and improvements you pay for after inheriting.
  • Report the sale on Form 8949 and Schedule D, and watch for Form 1099-S from the title company.
  • Rental depreciation taken after May 6, 1997 is treated differently, so tell your preparer if the house was a rental.

Does an inherited Utah house go through probate before it sells?

Usually yes, because a Utah house titled in the deceased person's name needs someone with court authority, called a personal representative, to sign the sale.

Informal probate begins at the district court in the county of the person's home or property. Nothing can be filed until 120 hours (five days) after the death. The window closes three years after the death. The court then signs a Statement of Informal Probate. With a will you receive Letters Testamentary, and without one you receive Letters of Administration.

Informal probate in Utah
StepRequirement
Earliest filing120 hours after death
Latest filingWithin three years of death
Who filesApplicant at least 21 years old
WhereDistrict court in the county of residence or property
What you receiveLetters Testamentary or Letters of Administration

The personal representative's duties include collecting and inventorying the estate, paying taxes and mortgages on real property, making repairs where needed, filing estate and income tax returns, and selling property if needed to pay taxes or debts.

Who is appointed to sign for the estate

The court works down a priority list and appoints the first person on it who is willing and at least 21 years old.

  • A person nominated in the will.
  • The spouse, if the will makes a gift to the spouse.
  • Anyone receiving a gift under the will.
  • The spouse, even without a gift or without a will.
  • Any heir.
  • Any creditor, but only after 45 days following the death.

Someone with the same or higher priority can sign a Renunciation to back the applicant. Publishing a notice to creditors is optional, though publication shortens the creditor claim period to about three months, compared with up to one year without it. If you plan to sell the house, ask the attorney or clerk whether the representative needs further court approval before signing a purchase contract, since that depends on the will and the estate.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Utah houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If the family disagrees about the house

A disagreement moves the case from informal to formal probate, which is slower and usually calls for an attorney.

If an interested person will not sign the Waiver of Notice, the court must set a hearing. A written objection also makes the case formal, and after one is filed all parties must attend mediation and exchange initial disclosures. Formal probate is beyond what the court's self-help pages cover, so find legal help.

A small estate affidavit does not solve the house problem. That route applies to personal property under $100,000, waits 30 days after death, and cannot transfer Utah real property such as a home.

Property tax break after the owner dies

The 45 percent primary residential exemption does not carry over to heirs on its own, so the home can be taxed at its full market value until someone applies.

A qualifying primary home is taxed on 55 percent of fair market value. New owners do not inherit the exemption automatically. Starting January 1, 2027, a deed or trust transfer calls for a new Form TC-473A under 2026 SB 238. Send the application to the county Board of Equalization by September 15. A late one is refused.

Heirs who sell quickly may never need this. Heirs who keep a vacant house for a year should ask the county assessor what it requires.

A short plan for selling an inherited house

Begin with who holds title. A house still in the deceased owner's name calls for an informal probate filing, and you should wait for the Letters before signing a listing or purchase contract. Meanwhile, order the date-of-death appraisal and collect the mortgage statement, tax bill and homeowners insurance information.

A buyer paying cash can close soon after the Letters are issued and the title company clears the file, since no lender has to approve the deal. Check with the title company early about which court papers it wants, so the closing date holds.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Utah inheritance tax?

No. The state's inheritance tax ended after December 31, 2004, no return is required, and no inheritance tax waiver is needed.

Does Utah have an estate tax?

No. Utah has only the old pick-up tax that was repealed, and the federal estate tax applies to estates above $13,990,000 for 2025 deaths or $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths.

Do heirs pay income tax when they sell an inherited Utah house?

Only on gain above the stepped-up basis, which is generally the fair market value on the date of death. A sale near that value often leaves little or no taxable gain.

How long after a death can I start informal probate in Utah?

You can file 120 hours (five days) after death, and the case must be filed within three years of death. Use the district court in the county where the person lived or held property.

Can a small estate affidavit transfer a Utah house?

No. The affidavit route applies to personal property under $100,000 and excludes Utah real property, so a house usually needs probate or another title transfer.

Steps in the Utah eviction process

A Utah eviction runs in this order: a written notice, a court complaint and summons, the tenant's response window, an occupancy hearing or a default, and finally an order of restitution that a sheriff or constable enforces. Only a court order can lawfully remove a tenant.

A landlord may not change the locks, shut off utilities or remove a tenant's belongings to force a move. Skipping the court steps can turn a simple nonpayment case into a damages claim against the owner.

For a seller, the useful point is timing. The case has several fixed clocks, and the sections below put them in one place.

Which notice to serve first

The notice depends on why the landlord wants possession. Utah Code 78B-6-802 sets the periods, and each situation has a numbered court form.

Notice periods by situation
SituationNotice periodWhat the tenant can do
Unpaid rent or other amounts due3 business days after service, pay or surrenderPay the amount demanded and keep the lease
Other lease covenant not kept3 calendar days after service, perform or surrenderFix the problem within the notice period
Improper sublet, waste, unlawful business, nuisance or criminal act3 calendar days quit noticeCure where the problem can be cured
Month-to-month (indefinite, periodic rent)Served at least 15 calendar days before the end of the periodLeave by the end of the period
Tenancy at willAt least 5 calendar daysLeave when the notice runs out
Fixed term that has endedNo notice needed under the statuteLeave at the end of the term

Business days leave out weekends and court holidays. Calendar days count every day. A landlord who counts the wrong way can lose a week and have to start over.

The forms are separate for each ground: 1001EV for the three-day pay or vacate notice, 1005EV for a violation the tenant can fix, 1035EV for one the tenant cannot fix, 1050EV for the five-day no-lease notice, and 1015EV or 1015.5EV for nuisance.

Delivering the eviction notice

Under Utah Code 78B-6-805, a notice can be handed to the tenant, sent by registered or certified mail, left with a suitable person at the home, or posted in a conspicuous place on the property if nobody suitable can be found.

Each tenant gets their own copy, and the landlord keeps the original.

  • Hand delivery to the tenant.
  • Registered or certified mail.
  • Leaving it with another adult at the home, or posting it on the door.
  • Keep the date, method and the name of whoever served it.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Utah house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Can the tenant fix the problem and stay?

Yes. Subsection 2 of 78B-6-802 says that during the notice period the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the term or another interested person may cure the violation and keep the lease alive.

Where a violation under the subletting, unlawful business, nuisance or criminal act grounds cannot be cured, the landlord may still give the notice. That is why the court has one form for fixable problems and another for problems that cannot be fixed.

After the notice period ends

If the tenant has not complied, the landlord files a complaint and summons with the district court and serves them on the tenant. The landlord cannot serve the papers personally.

The filing set is a cover sheet, a summons (1105EV), a complaint (1100EV), a COVID eviction declaration (2200EV) and a disclosure notice (1150EV), with the lease and the notice attached as exhibits. Papers can be filed in person, by email as a PDF, or by mail, which is the slowest.

  • Service must be done by an adult who is not part of the case, a sheriff or constable for a fee, or a process server.
  • Papers must be served within 120 days of filing.
  • The tenant generally has 3 business days after service to answer, counted from the day after service.

Occupancy hearing and default

If the tenant answers, even late, the landlord cannot take a default and must request an occupancy hearing on form 1180EV. The court schedules that hearing within 10 days of the request.

At the hearing the judge decides who may stay while the case goes on and whether it can be decided at once or needs a trial. A judge who sides with the landlord signs an order of restitution. If more information is needed, a trial follows within 60 days.

If the tenant never answers, the landlord first checks military status on the SCRA website. A tenant in the military can get a delay of up to 90 days. Then the landlord files a default certificate and an ex parte motion for an order of restitution.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Utah houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How long the tenant has to leave, and who enforces it

Under Utah Code 78B-6-812 the tenant has three calendar days after service of the order of restitution to vacate. Only a sheriff, deputy, police officer, constable, state investigator or private investigator may serve it.

If the tenant stays, a sheriff or constable acting at the landlord's direction may enter by force using the least destructive means possible. A tenant's request for a hearing about enforcement does not pause the removal unless the tenant posts a bond or certified funds approved by the court and the court orders a stay. When a hearing is requested, the court must set it within 10 calendar days.

  • Serve the complaint after filing: within 120 days.
  • Tenant answer period: 3 business days after service.
  • Occupancy hearing: set within 10 days of the request.
  • Military delay, if applicable: up to 90 days.
  • Tenant leaves after the order: 3 calendar days after service.
  • Access to essential belongings: within 5 business days.
  • Belongings treated as abandoned: after 15 calendar days.

The tenant's belongings and unpaid rent

After an eviction the landlord must give the tenant reasonable access within 5 business days, free of charge, to essentials such as clothing, identification, financial and employment papers and medical items. Other belongings can be stored at reasonable cost and are treated as abandoned if unclaimed after 15 calendar days.

A landlord can also ask for a money judgment. Utah Code 78B-6-811 provides for rent plus three times the damages assessed in listed categories, including unlawful detainer, waste that was pleaded and proven, and amounts due under the contract. The court must award costs and reasonable attorney fees to the winning side.

A motion to increase the judgment must be filed within 180 days of when restitution is enforced or the tenant leaves.

How eviction affects selling a rented house in Utah

A pending eviction does not have to stop a sale, but it changes what a buyer will pay attention to. Call the court clerk or a Utah attorney before closing to find out what happens to a filed case when the owner sells.

  • Gather the lease, every notice served and proof of service.
  • Keep the rent ledger and security deposit record together.
  • Note which court dates are set.
  • Remember that showings need 24 hours notice to the tenant unless the rental agreement says otherwise.

Owners who inherited a rental, fell behind on a mortgage or do not want to wait through a hearing calendar sometimes sell as-is with the tenant still in place. Cash Home Buyers can look at a tenant-occupied Utah house and explain what an as-is sale would involve.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

If the rental is being foreclosed on

Tenants in a foreclosed rental have extra protection. Utah Code 78B-6-901.5 tells tenants that, under federal law, they may stay until the lease ends or until 90 days after the sale, whichever is later. They must keep paying rent and following the lease.

For a trust deed sale, Utah Code 57-1-25 requires a notice of sale posted at least 20 days before the sale, with the last newspaper publication 10 to 30 days before it. Where the loan financed a residential rental, the notice must also be posted on the unit doors or mailed to the occupants, with a tenant statement in at least 14 point type.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an eviction take in Utah?

It depends on whether the tenant answers. The notice period runs 3 business days for unpaid rent, 5 calendar days for a tenancy at will and 15 calendar days for month-to-month. After that, the tenant has 3 business days to answer the complaint, an occupancy hearing is set within 10 days of a request, and the tenant has 3 calendar days to leave after the order. A trial adds more time.

Can a Utah landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. Only a court order allows a lawful eviction, and changing locks, shutting off utilities or removing a tenant's property is prohibited.

What is the 3-day notice in Utah?

It is the written notice to pay or surrender used for unpaid rent. Under Utah Code 78B-6-802 the tenant has three business days after service to pay what is demanded or give up possession. A tenant who pays in full during that window can keep the lease.

What can a landlord recover from an evicted tenant in Utah?

Unpaid rent, damages and court costs, and in some categories up to three times the actual damages. Utah Code 78B-6-811 provides for treble damages on listed items, and the landlord must prove them.

Can I sell my Utah rental house while the tenant is still there?

Yes, an owner can list or sell a tenant-occupied house, though entry for showings requires at least 24 hours notice unless the rental agreement says otherwise. Before you sign, ask the court clerk or a Utah attorney how a sale affects any pending eviction case. Cash Home Buyers can buy as-is with the tenant in place.

title: Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House
content:
Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Cash Home Buyers in Utah
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Utah House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Utah?
We buy Utah houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Utah have its own capital gains tax on a house sale?

No. Utah does not run a separate capital gains tax, so any taxable gain from selling a house is simply part of your income and taxed at the state's flat individual income tax rate.

For 2025 that rate is 4.5 percent, down from 4.55 percent after the 2025 Legislature passed HB 106. Line 4 of the Utah TC-40 starts from your federal adjusted gross income, which already includes any gain you report on your federal return. So the question for a Utah seller is mostly a federal one: how much of the gain survives the home sale exclusion?

The Legislature sets the rate and can change it from one tax year to the next, so read the instructions for the year you sell.

The home sale exclusion

A single seller can exclude up to $250,000 of gain on a main home, and married couples filing jointly can exclude up to $500,000.

Two tests apply to the five years before closing: you owned the home for 24 months and lived in it as your main home for 24 months. The two stretches can fall at different times. Couples filing jointly need only one spouse to pass the ownership test, but both must pass the use test. Taking the exclusion on a different home sale within the past two years generally rules it out.

  • Single: up to $250,000 excluded.
  • Married filing jointly: up to $500,000 excluded.
  • Ownership: 24 months within the last 5 years.
  • Use as main home: 24 months (730 days) within the last 5 years.
  • Look-back: no other home sale excluded in the prior 2 years.

A surviving spouse keeps the $500,000 limit if the sale closes within two years of the spouse's death and the other conditions are met. IRS Publication 523 covers the fine print.

Working out the gain

Gain is the sale price minus selling expenses, minus your adjusted basis, which is what you paid plus qualifying improvements.

  • Amount realized: the selling price less selling expenses.
  • Basis: the purchase cost plus improvements that add value, prolong the home's life or adapt it to a new use. Repairs count only as part of a larger improvement project.
  • Closing costs: items such as recording fees, survey fees and owner's title insurance can be added to basis. Mortgage points and loan fees cannot.
  • Inherited homes: basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date if the estate chose it.
  • Gifted homes: basis is generally the donor's adjusted basis.

Save the closing statement from when you bought, plus receipts for any addition, new roof or remodel. A finished basement or a new roof can change the taxable number noticeably, and a CPA can tie the figures together before you list.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Utah house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

When the exclusion falls short

The exclusion does not cover rental depreciation, periods when the house was not your main home, or a separate business portion of the property.

Depreciation adjustments taken after May 6, 1997 for business or rental use must be recaptured, and you cannot exclude the part of gain equal to them. Gain tied to nonqualified use after 2008, when the property was not your main home, generally cannot be excluded either. Depreciation recapture goes on Form 4797.

A partial exclusion is available if you sold before reaching 24 months for a qualifying reason:

  • A work move at least 50 miles farther from the home.
  • A health-related move.
  • An unforeseeable event such as death, divorce or unemployment.

Homes acquired in a like-kind (section 1031) exchange within the past five years are barred from the exclusion altogether. Service members and certain Foreign Service or intelligence community members on qualified official extended duty can elect to suspend the five-year test period for up to 10 years. In an installment sale, the exclusion stays available even if you defer part of the gain.

A capital loss on a reportable sale can be deducted up to $3,000 a year against other income ($1,500 if married filing separately), with the rest carried forward. Ask your tax preparer whether a loss on a personal residence qualifies.

Federal rates on the taxable part

Federal tax on gain from a house owned longer than one year is 0, 15 or 20 percent, and unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property tops out at 25 percent.

2025 long-term capital gains brackets
Filing status0% rate up to15% rate up to
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700

Anything above the 15 percent ceiling is taxed at 20 percent. Selling after a year or less of ownership produces short-term gain, which is taxed like wages. Higher earners can also owe the 3.8 percent net investment income tax, which applies when modified adjusted gross income passes $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for joint filers. Home sale gain escapes that tax only to the extent it is excluded from regular income tax.

If you left Utah or live elsewhere

If you moved out or live in another state, you report the sale on the Utah return with Schedule TC-40B. Utah taxes what you earned as a resident, plus Utah-source income after you left.

Selling a Utah house from another state still counts as Utah-source income. A nonresident with a federal filing requirement must file in Utah too, entering the full federal amount on line 4 before the schedule splits out the Utah share.

Utah also offers a taxpayer tax credit equal to 6 percent of a base amount that phases out as income rises, with the phase-out starting at $18,213 for single filers and $36,426 for joint filers. The capital gain transactions credit on the form relates to certain Utah small business stock investments, so it is not a home sale break.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Utah houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Reporting the sale and due dates

A home sale goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D. Report it if you received Form 1099-S, even when the whole gain is excluded, and report it whenever part of the gain is taxable.

The Utah return and payment are due each April 15. An extension of up to six months moves the return to October 15 but does not extend the time to pay, so interest and penalties can still apply.

If you sell this year, set aside the estimated tax before you spend the proceeds, and ask a CPA or enrolled agent whether quarterly estimates are needed. We can close on your timeline if you need the sale to land in a particular tax year.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Utah capital gains tax rate for real estate?

There is no separate rate. Utah taxes capital gains as ordinary income at its flat individual rate, which is 4.5 percent for 2025.

Do I owe Utah tax if the gain is under the $250,000 exclusion?

Usually not. Utah starts from federal adjusted gross income, so gain that is fully excluded federally does not raise the Utah taxable amount, though a 1099-S still has to be reported.

Does selling an inherited Utah house trigger capital gains?

Only on gain above the stepped-up basis. The basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, so a sale soon after can show little or no gain.

What if I rented my Utah house before selling?

Depreciation you took after May 6, 1997 cannot be excluded and is recaptured, and gain tied to periods when the house was not your main home may also be taxable. Ask a tax professional how your rental years affect the figures.

Do I pay Utah tax on a house I sold from another state?

If the house is in Utah, the sale is Utah-source income and a nonresident must file when there is a federal filing requirement. Schedule TC-40B apportions the tax.

Utah Tax Sales: Redemption and Selling Before the Sale

Cash Home Buyers in Utah
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Utah Tax Sales: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Utah Tax Sales sale
  • Turn the Utah Tax Sales offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Utah House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Utah?
We buy Utah houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How a Utah tax sale works from start to finish

A Utah tax sale is a county auction of real property whose taxes have stayed unpaid for four years. The county doesn't take the house at the first missed payment. It moves through a fixed sequence, and the owner can stop the process at almost any point before the auction by paying what is owed.

StageWhat happens
DelinquencyTax unpaid after the November 30 due date, then penalty and interest
Four years passProperty not redeemed by the following March 15 goes on the tax sale listing
NoticeAuditor mails notice to the owner, any occupant and other interests of record
SalePublic auction in May or June, in person or online
DeedCounty auditor issues a tax deed after the governing body accepts the bid

Delinquency and the cost of waiting

Taxes are delinquent if paid or postmarked after November 30, or the next business day when that date lands on a weekend or holiday. From there the cost grows in steps under Utah Code 59-2-1331.

  • A penalty of 2.5% of the delinquent amount or $10, whichever is greater, or 1% if everything is paid by January 31.
  • Interest from the following January 1 at 6% plus the federal funds target rate, held between 7% and 10%.
  • Added interest for each later year of delinquency, until the account is settled by redemption or sale.

Tax notice charges count too. A delinquent charge such as an unpaid special district fee or assessment can start the same clock as unpaid tax under 59-2-1317.

When a delinquent property goes on the tax sale list

The county treasurer lists property for sale if it is still not redeemed by March 15 following four years from the date the tax or charge became delinquent. Utah Code 59-2-1343 then has the treasurer file that tax sale listing with the county auditor.

A deferred tax or charge becomes delinquent only if full payment isn't made before the five-year deferral period ends.

The long runway is why many owners are surprised. The bill may have sat unpaid for years with no one living in the house, while the notices went to an old address.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Utah house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How an owner can redeem before the sale

Anyone can redeem on behalf of the record owner at any time before the sale by paying the county treasurer every delinquent tax, tax notice charge, interest amount, penalty and administrative cost. Utah Code 59-2-1346 lets someone other than the owner pay, which helps when a relative or lender steps in.

Before the redemption period ends, the treasurer must accept payments of at least $10 on account, with any final payment allowed in any amount. Payments are applied to the most recent year first, starting with interest and administrative costs, then penalty, then tax. In Salt Lake County, partial payments do not redeem a property, and redemption within roughly three weeks of the sale must be paid in cash or bank-certified funds.

Redemption leaves ownership unchanged. The deed stays in the current owner's name and the account is cleared.

Can the county reduce or defer what is owed?

In some cases, yes. Utah Code 59-2-1347 lets a county legislative body accept less than the full amount or defer the tax when it finds that the best human interests and the interests of the state and county are served.

The applicant describes the property, its current value, the delinquent taxes, interest and penalties, and the amount proposed to be paid or deferred. The county can't grant a deferral without written consent from the holder of any mortgage or trust deed. Deferred tax is recorded as a lien that bears interest and is due when the property is sold or otherwise conveyed. A deferral can slow things down, but the balance still has to be paid at closing.

Notice of a tax sale

The county auditor must send notice by certified and first class mail, or first class mail plus a tracked delivery service, to the last known recorded owner, the occupant of any improved property, and other interests of record as of the preceding March 15. The mailing rules are in Utah Code 59-2-1351.

Public notice depends on the county's class.

  • First class county: notice on the county website at least four weeks before the sale, plus a newspaper ad with the web address.
  • Other classes: a newspaper notice once a week for the four weeks before the sale, or five public postings if the county has no newspaper, plus the state public notice site.

The notice names the last known owner, the parcel number and the legal description. It warns that bids below the total taxes, charges, interest, penalty and costs will not be accepted.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Utah houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens at the auction

The auditor offers the parcels at public auction and sells each to the highest bidder for cash, in May or June. The sale can take place at the front door of the county courthouse or through an electronic process that matches the in-person format, so the public can watch and bid.

Formats vary by county. Salt Lake County has run its sale online through Public Surplus, with bidders registering about a week ahead and posting a $500 deposit by wire. Check your county auditor's site for the date and rules.

The governing body may accept the highest bid for the whole parcel, or a bid that pays all taxes and costs for a smaller piece of the parcel. It must reject bids on a thin strip around the perimeter or on a strip that cuts off access to the rest. The county legislative body can also decide that none of the bids is acceptable.

The winning bidder and any extra money

The bidder receives a tax deed conveying the property in fee simple, issued by the county auditor and recorded by the county recorder. Under Utah Code 59-2-1351.1, the deed recites the total paid, the years of assessment and delinquency, the property description and the buyer's name.

A bidder can't back out once the sale of a parcel is closed. The county can enforce the bid by judgment, plus interest and attorney fees. Any money above what is needed to cover taxes, charges, penalties, interest and costs is treated as unclaimed property under the state's unclaimed property act. Salt Lake County issues its deed within 60 days, after the county council ratifies the sale.

If a tax title later proves invalid, the purchaser holds a lien for the amount paid, up to the taxes, interest and penalties, under 59-2-1352.

Selling a Utah house before the tax sale

Until the auction, the owner still holds title and can sell, and the delinquent balance is paid out of the sale. The buyer or title company requests a payoff from the county treasurer, and the payoff must cover tax, tax notice charges, interest, penalty and costs.

Timing is the main constraint. Because the sale is held in May or June and redemption must be completed beforehand, an owner who waits until the notice arrives may have limited time. A cash purchase that closes quickly can fit that window, and the owner doesn't need to repair the house first.

  • Ask the county treasurer for a written payoff amount and its good-through date.
  • Confirm whether any deferral lien or assessment charge is on the bill.
  • Check the county auditor's calendar for the exact sale date.
You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Common problems for owners facing a tax sale

Problems at this stage tend to stack up. These are the usual ones.

  • Unopened mail, since notices go to the last known address.
  • An estate that hasn't been probated, so no one has authority to pay or sell.
  • Back taxes plus a mortgage, which both come out of any sale.
  • Little cash for the redemption amount in one payment.

Utah's redemption statute lets installments of at least $10 count toward the balance, but the full amount must be paid before the sale. A buyer can't erase the debt, only pay it at closing.

Frequently asked questions

How long before a Utah tax sale can I still redeem my property?

Up to the sale itself. Utah Code 59-2-1346 allows redemption at any time before the sale, which is held in May or June after four years of delinquency. Pay the full amount to the county treasurer.

How many years of unpaid taxes lead to a Utah tax sale?

Four. A property not redeemed by March 15 following four years from the date the tax or charge became delinquent is placed on the tax sale listing under Utah Code 59-2-1343.

Does a Utah tax sale buyer get clear ownership?

The auditor issues a tax deed conveying the property in fee simple, and the deed is prima facie evidence that the proceedings were regular. If the tax title is later found invalid, the buyer has a lien for the amount paid.

What happens to extra bid money at a Utah tax sale?

Money above the taxes, charges, penalty, interest and costs is treated as unclaimed property under Utah's unclaimed property act. The county doesn't keep it.

Can I sell my house if it is already on the Utah tax sale list?

Yes, as long as the sale hasn't happened. The unpaid balance is paid from the proceeds at closing, so get a payoff figure from the county treasurer first and check the auction date with the county auditor.

Utah Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in Utah

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Utah Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale

Selling a Utah House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Utah houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

When a Utah estate has to go through probate

A Utah estate needs probate when it includes real property of any value, or when its other assets are worth more than $100,000. For anyone who inherited a house, that is the starting point.

The house usually forces the issue. A bank account or a car can sometimes be collected with a short affidavit, but land and buildings can't. If the person who died owned a home in their own name, someone needs court authority before the title can move to an heir or a buyer.

  • Real property of any value: probate is required.
  • Other assets above $100,000, not counting land or cars: probate is required.
  • Smaller estates with no real property: a small estate affidavit may be enough.

Can a small estate affidavit transfer a Utah house?

No. The Utah small estate affidavit covers personal property only. It can't be used to transfer title to land or a house.

Under Utah Code 75-3-1201, a successor can present an affidavit to a bank or other holder 30 days after the death. The affidavit states that the whole estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000, that 30 days have gone by, that no one has applied to be personal representative, and that the person claiming is entitled to the property. It is signed before a notary and handed to the third party. Nothing is filed with the court.

The same section lets the Motor Vehicle Division retitle up to four boats, motor vehicles, trailers or semitrailers on that kind of affidavit. Water company shares are excluded. None of this reaches the deed to a house, so heirs holding a house still need an appointed personal representative or another court-approved route.

Which court handles the case

Probate is filed in a Utah district court, in the county where the person lived at death or, if they didn't live in Utah, in any county where they owned property. Utah Code 75-3-201 sets that venue rule, and later proceedings generally stay in the court where the first one was filed.

Filing practice differs by place. Papers for a case in Utah County go to the Provo Courthouse, delivered in person or emailed to the filing address the court lists. Check with the clerk in your county before you file.

Venue matters for a sale because the court that appoints the personal representative is the one that issues the letters a title company will ask to see. If the owner lived in Salt Lake City but the inherited house is in a rural county, the case is normally opened where the owner lived.

Who can be the personal representative?

Any person aged 21 or older who isn't found unsuitable can serve, and Utah ranks who gets first claim on the job. The order in Utah Code 75-3-203 runs like this.

  1. The person named in a probated will.
  2. A surviving spouse who is also a devisee.
  3. Other devisees.
  4. A surviving spouse who is not a devisee.
  5. Other heirs.
  6. Any creditor, once 45 days after the death.

People with equal or higher priority can sign a renunciation so another family member can take the role. Anyone with priority can also nominate a qualified person. Family disagreements tend to surface here, and one heir who won't sign can turn an informal case into a formal one with a hearing.

Informal probate step by step

Informal probate asks the court to appoint a personal representative without a hearing. It works best when every interested person agrees. For a case with no objections, you gather these documents.

  • Application to be appointed, with the filing fee and the district court probate cover sheet.
  • Waiver of notice signed by interested persons such as heirs, devisees, spouses and creditors.
  • Renunciation forms from anyone with equal or higher priority who is stepping aside.
  • An official death certificate.
  • Acceptance of appointment signed by the applicant.
  • The original will, if there is one.

If the clerk approves, the court signs a Statement of Informal Probate and issues Letters Testamentary when there is a will, or Letters of Administration when there isn't. Order certified copies, since banks, insurers and title companies each tend to want one. If an interested person won't sign the waiver, a hearing is needed and the case becomes formal.

If nobody opens probate within three years

Under Utah Code 75-3-107, an informal probate or formal testacy proceeding generally may not start more than three years after the death. If no will is probated in that time, the presumption of intestacy becomes final.

The court keeps some power after that point. It can still decide what property the decedent owned and can appoint a personal representative, but certain claims, including homestead and family allowances and most creditor claims other than administration expenses, can't be presented. Families past the three-year mark should talk to a probate attorney about determining heirs.

Houses are where this bites. A property that sat untitled after a parent's death, with taxes accruing, can be hard to sell until the paperwork catches up.

Creditors and a house sold from an estate

Creditors have a limited window to make claims, and the personal representative controls how that window is opened. After appointment, the representative may publish a notice once a week for three weeks in a county newspaper. It tells creditors to present claims within three months of first publication or be barred (75-3-801).

Publishing is optional. A representative may skip it, though it makes sense when the debts aren't all known. Without notice, 75-3-803 still bars most claims that arose before death one year after the death. Mortgages and other liens on the property are not wiped out by these time limits, so a house with a loan still has to be paid off or assumed at sale.

Can the personal representative sell the inherited house?

Yes. A personal representative acting reasonably for the benefit of the interested persons may sell, mortgage or lease any real or personal property of the estate, for cash, credit or part of each (Utah Code 75-3-714(23)).

Those powers begin when the representative is appointed, so a family can't sign a sale contract in the estate's name before the letters issue. A related section treats some acts that benefit the estate before appointment as if they came after, but a buyer or title company will still want the letters in hand.

The same part of the code lets a representative repair buildings, insure estate assets, pay taxes and assessments, and hire agents or attorneys. In practice the estate can keep the heat on, pay the property tax bill and clean out the house while a sale is arranged.

Buyer protection after an heir sells

A good-faith buyer who pays value for property distributed by a personal representative takes title free of other estate claimants. Utah Code 75-3-910 protects a purchaser or lender who deals with a distributee holding a deed of distribution, even if the distribution was improper or the representative's authority had already ended.

The buyer doesn't have to investigate whether the representative acted properly. That is part of why heirs often sign a deed of distribution first and sell afterward, or sell directly through the representative while the estate is open.

Common snags for sellers of inherited houses

Sellers of inherited houses in Utah most often lose time on paperwork rather than on the sale itself. A few patterns repeat.

  • Heirs live in different states and one won't sign a waiver, which sends the case to a hearing.
  • The house is empty, so utilities, insurance and yard upkeep fall on the estate until closing.
  • The title still shows the person who died, and no representative has been appointed.
  • Property tax bills keep arriving at the old mailing address.
  • The home needs repairs that no heir wants to fund.

A cash buyer can purchase the house as it stands, which spares the estate repairs and showings. The seller side still needs the court steps above: letters first, then a deed from the representative.

Frequently asked questions

Is probate required in Utah if the house has a mortgage?

Yes, if the house is in the decedent's name. Probate is required whenever the estate includes real property of any value, and the mortgage stays attached to the property either way.

How soon after a death can I file for informal probate in Utah?

Five days. An informal case may not be filed until 120 hours after the death, under Utah Code 75-3-307.

How long do I have to start probate in Utah?

Generally three years from the date of death under Utah Code 75-3-107. After that the court can still decide who owned what, but you should talk to a probate attorney.

Can heirs sell a Utah house without opening probate?

Usually not if the title is still in the decedent's name. The small estate affidavit doesn't cover real property, so a personal representative generally has to be appointed before a deed can be signed.

Does a Utah personal representative need court approval to sell the house?

Not always. Utah Code 75-3-714 lets a representative sell estate real property, subject to the will and any court order. If the will limits the power or an heir objects in a formal case, the court may need to approve it.
